name: Brali editorial normalization register
description: Reviewed corrections applied to inherited source content before public pages, evidence classification, indexing, and trusted feeds are generated.

rules.reason: The inherited sentence presents a fixed-looking 21-66 day range that is not supported by the cited habit-formation literature. The replacement removes unsupported precision rather than substituting another universal countdown.
rules.replacement: There is no fixed number of days for a habit to become automatic. Keep the context consistent, notice whether the action is getting easier to repeat, and review the practice over time instead of treating a countdown as a success criterion.

rules.reason: This inherited site-wide paragraph fragment is obsolete product identity and duplicated template copy. It adds no protocol-specific value and exposes the pre-Brali MetalHatsCats positioning in search-facing canonical content. Remove it rather than replacing it with a new repeated boilerplate.

This repeated mini-app sentence belongs to the previous product identity and is not protocol-specific content. It appears both adjacent to and separated from the MetalHatsCats boilerplate, so it is normalized independently.

A smaller set of inherited pages embeds the old mini-app positioning inside otherwise unique introductory sentences. Remove the sentence containing that obsolete product mechanic while preserving the surrounding protocol-specific prose.

The old app CTA sends readers to the pre-Brali MetalHatsCats route and repeats obsolete product positioning. Remove the entire CTA paragraph rather than exposing a stale brand/domain or inventing an unverified replacement workflow.

Some structured source fields still carry the pre-Brali LifeOS domain even after visible legacy CTA cleanup. Preserve the useful deep link while moving it to the maintained canonical Brali site so old product identity cannot leak into generated metadata or search surfaces.
Flame Counter is a residual mechanic from the previous product identity. Keep the surrounding protocol content but replace the obsolete mechanic label with a neutral description.

The repeated closing cluster is an obsolete legacy-app call to action and a self-referencing link, not protocol-specific content. It was previously hidden because the whole article body was discarded; with long-form articles restored, the CTA sentence cluster is removed while the surrounding article is preserved.

A closing-variant of the legacy MetalHatsCats product-intro boilerplate that the existing product-intro rule does not catch because of its leading 'We will close by repeating' wrapper. It is obsolete product identity copy, not protocol-specific guidance.

The sentence ends with a call to use a legacy companion app that is not a current Brali product. The consistency advice stands on its own; the app reference is removed instead of implying an available download.
rules.replacement: Focus on consistency rather than perfection to build momentum.

rules.reason: The inherited FAQ answer routes readers into the retired Life OS app. The replacement keeps the tracking advice while removing the nonexistent-product reference.
rules.replacement: Use the check-in method described above and record the result somewhere you will actually review, so progress stays visible over time.

rules.reason: A family of inherited sentences tells readers to log results in the Brali LifeOS app. Brali publishes data sources and protocols, not a consumer app, so the logging advice is repointed to tools the reader already has.
rules.replacement: $1 in a journal, note, or tracker you already use

rules.reason: These call-to-action fragments exist only to send readers to a legacy app listing or self-referencing page. They carry no protocol content, so they are removed rather than rewritten.
The sentence describes a legacy app workspace that is not a current Brali product. Removing it avoids implying an available application while leaving the surrounding guidance intact.
Bare leftover variant of the legacy app CTA that remained after the earlier CTA-cluster rule because it lacks the workspace sentence and link. Same obsolete product reference, same removal.
Legacy app call-to-action with a trailing self-referencing link. The app is not a current Brali product, so the whole CTA is removed.

Prose sentences end with a colon and a self-referencing canonical link left over from app-link CTAs. The lookbehind requires a word character before the colon, so JSON key-value syntax can never match. The link adds no protocol content and is removed.
Tool lists offered the legacy app as one option beside paper. Collapsing the option keeps the instruction natural without implying an available application.
Sentence-initial references to the legacy app as a tool become a generic reader-owned tool. Brali publishes protocols and data sources, not a consumer app.

Mid-sentence references to the legacy app as the place to act, log, or check in are repointed to tools the reader already has. This preserves the practical instruction while removing the nonexistent-product reference.
Standalone narrative sentences about opening or closing the legacy app describe a product that does not exist. Removing them keeps the surrounding narrative intact.
Equipment lists name the legacy app as required gear, including a '(free)' availability claim. Brali has no consumer app, so the item becomes a generic phone-or-notebook requirement.
The sentence promises an in-app follow-up interaction Brali does not operate. Removed rather than replaced with an unverifiable alternative.
Standalone closing CTA sending readers to track the practice in the legacy app. Removed; the article body already explains how to observe progress.
Legacy structured how-to step title telling readers to check in via the retired Brali LifeOS app. The step summary already points to a personal journal or tracker; the title now matches that meaning.
rules.replacement: Check in and log your result
